prompt: A goods transport agency in Nagpur, Maharashtra, moves cargo from Nagpur to Kolkata for a manufacturer registered in Raipur, Chhattisgarh. Freight is Rs 64,500 and the GTA has not opted for forward charge. What is the tax and who pays it?
completion:
The manufacturer pays integrated GST (IGST) of Rs 3,225 under reverse charge. For goods transport to a registered person, the place of supply is the recipient's location, Chhattisgarh; the GTA is in Maharashtra, so the supply is inter-state.
Freight 64,500 x 5% = Rs 3,225 IGST.
The goods transport agency (GTA) has not opted for forward charge, so the manufacturer, as a registered person, pays it under the reverse charge mechanism (RCM). It reports the amount in Table 3.1(d) of GSTR-3B and pays it in cash. The 5% rate carries no input tax credit for the GTA. Reference: Section 12(8)(a) of the IGST Act, 2017 and Section 9(3) of the CGST Act.
note: Sec 12(8)(a) IGST puts place of supply for goods transport to a registered person at the recipient's location (only the export proviso was omitted in 2023); Maharashtra to Chhattisgarh is inter-state; GTA 5% RCM with registered recipient, paid in cash, shown in 3.1(d). 64,500 x 5% = 3,225.

prompt: Our Indian branch office provides back-office services to our own head office in London and is paid in pounds. Is this an export of services?
completion:
No. A branch and its foreign head office are establishments of the same legal person, so the supply fails the fifth condition for export of services. Integrated GST (IGST) at 18% is payable. On a monthly billing of Rs 26,40,000 that is 26,40,000 x 18% = Rs 4,75,200. It cannot be zero-rated under a letter of undertaking (LUT).
If the Indian entity were a separately incorporated subsidiary of the London company, the supply would qualify as an export, provided the other conditions are met. Reference: Section 2(6)(v) and Explanation 1 to Section 8 of the IGST Act, 2017.
note: Sec 2(6)(v) IGST: supplier and recipient must not be merely establishments of a distinct person (Expl 1 to Sec 8); CBIC Circular 161/17/2021 confirms branch-to-foreign-HO supply is not export. 26,40,000 x 18% = 4,75,200.

prompt:
User: An IT unit in an SEZ in Gandhinagar bills an SEZ client with no GST under LUT.
Assistant: Yes, a supply to an SEZ unit for authorised operations is zero-rated.
User: The same unit now bills a client in Ahmedabad outside the SEZ Rs 6,20,000. What tax?
completion:
Charge integrated GST (IGST) of Rs 1,11,600. A supply by an SEZ unit is treated as inter-state, whoever the buyer is, so a sale to a client in the domestic tariff area (DTA) in Ahmedabad is not intra-state even though both are in Gujarat. It is also not zero-rated, because only supplies to an SEZ, or exports, qualify.
Fee 6,20,000 x 18% = Rs 1,11,600 IGST. Invoice total Rs 7,31,600.
The Ahmedabad client can claim the IGST as input tax credit (ITC). Reference: Section 7(5)(b) of the IGST Act, 2017.
note: Sec 7(5)(b) IGST makes supplies by an SEZ unit inter-state, so IGST applies on a sale to a DTA client. 6,20,000 x 18% = 1,11,600; total 7,31,600. Arithmetic correct.

prompt: A machinery dealer in Vadodara, Gujarat, sells a machine of Rs 48,00,000 (18%) to a buyer in Gujarat and also installs it at the buyer's plant in Daman. Which tax applies to the sale?
completion:
Charge integrated GST (IGST) of Rs 8,64,000. Where goods are assembled or installed at a site, the place of supply is the place of installation, here the Union territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu. The dealer is in Gujarat, so the supply is inter-state although the buyer's office is in Gujarat.
Value 48,00,000 x 18% = Rs 8,64,000 IGST. Invoice total Rs 56,64,000.
Show the Daman plant as the place of installation on the invoice. Reference: Section 10(1)(d) of the IGST Act, 2017.
note: Place of supply for goods installed at a site is the site (Sec 10(1)(d)); Gujarat to the Daman UT is inter-state; 48,00,000 x 18% = 8,64,000, total 56,64,000. The ITC-at-risk sentence is unsupported (IGST credit is claimable under the buyer's own registration), so removed.

prompt: A factory in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, employs 310 workers and must run a canteen under the Factories Act. The canteen contractor bills Rs 4,80,000 plus GST of Rs 24,000 a month. Can the factory claim the ITC?
completion:
Yes. The factory can claim the Rs 24,000 of input tax credit (ITC). Food and canteen services are normally blocked, but the block is lifted where the law obliges the employer to provide them. A factory with more than 250 workers must provide a canteen under Section 46 of the Factories Act, 1948.
Contractor bill: 4,80,000 x 5% = Rs 24,000 GST, fully claimable.
If the canteen were voluntary, the full Rs 24,000 would be blocked. Reference: proviso to Section 17(5)(b) of the CGST Act and CBIC Circular 172/04/2022-GST.
note: Circular 172/04/2022-GST says the proviso to Sec 17(5)(b) covers the whole clause, so canteen ITC is allowed where law makes it obligatory (Factories Act Sec 46, more than 250 workers); AARs agree. 4,80,000 x 5% = 24,000.

prompt: A BPO in Gurugram hires a 26-seater bus for staff pick-up at Rs 2,90,000 a month plus 18% GST. Can it claim ITC?
completion:
Yes. It can claim Rs 52,200 a month of input tax credit (ITC). Hire of a motor vehicle is blocked only for vehicles seating up to 13 persons, including the driver. A 26-seater bus is outside the block.
GST = 2,90,000 x 18% = Rs 52,200, eligible.
The credit is on the GST actually charged on the operator's tax invoice, whatever the rate, provided the usual conditions of Section 16 are met (invoice, receipt of service, tax paid, return filed). Reference: Section 17(5)(a) and 17(5)(b)(i) of the CGST Act.
note: Vehicles seating more than 13 are outside the Sec 17(5)(a) block, and hire is covered by 17(5)(b)(i). But the claim that credit depends on the operator charging 18% with credit is wrong: the recipient claims the GST actually charged. 2,90,000 x 18% = 52,200.

prompt: A car dealer in Indore uses 4 demo cars for test drives and later sells them. Is the GST on the demo cars blocked?
completion: No. The dealer can claim the input tax credit (ITC) on demo vehicles. The block on motor vehicles does not apply where the vehicle is used for further supply of such vehicles, and demo cars used for test drives are used in the business of selling cars. For example, ITC of Rs 1,42,000 a car on 4 cars = Rs 5,68,000 is eligible. When a demo car is later sold, the dealer charges GST on the sale at the rate in force then. If a demo car is capitalised and depreciation is claimed on the tax component, the ITC is lost under Section 16(3). Reference: Section 17(5)(a)(A) of the CGST Act, Circular 231/25/2024-GST as modified by Circular 262/08/2026-GST.
note: Conclusion right: Circular 262/08/2026-GST (26 Oct 2026) withdrew para 4.6 of Circular 231/25/2024-GST and confirms demo-vehicle ITC is not blocked under 17(5)(a)(A); capitalised vehicles need no depreciation on tax (Sec 16(3)). 4 x 1,42,000 = 5,68,000. Reference updated.

prompt: A dealer in Ahmedabad sells a diesel SUV, 4,395 mm long with a 1,956 cc engine, for Rs 18,40,000 before tax. What GST applies?
completion:
Charge 40% GST: Rs 7,36,000. From 22 September 2025, cars outside the small-car limits are taxed at 40% with no compensation cess. Small-car limits: length up to 4,000 mm, with engine up to 1,200 cc for petrol, LPG or CNG, or up to 1,500 cc for diesel. This SUV exceeds both length and engine size.
Value 18,40,000 x 40% = Rs 7,36,000.
Invoice total = Rs 25,76,000.
A buyer generally cannot claim input tax credit (ITC) on a motor vehicle under Section 17(5)(a), except for specified uses such as further supply or passenger or goods transport. Reference: Notification 9/2025-Central Tax (Rate) and Notification 2/2025-Compensation Cess (Rate).
note: 40% with nil cess from 22 Sep 2025 and small-car limits (4,000 mm; 1,200 cc petrol / 1,500 cc diesel) are right and arithmetic checks (18,40,000 x 40% = 7,36,000; total 25,76,000). The flat statement that a buyer cannot claim ITC is too broad (Section 17(5)(a) has exceptions) and the reference was vague.

prompt: A director of our company is a practising lawyer and bills us Rs 2,50,000 for drafting contracts, in his capacity as an advocate. Is this reverse charge as director services?
completion:
Yes, reverse charge still applies, but under the entry for legal services, not director services. The director entry covers services he supplies as a director. Drafting work as an advocate falls under legal services by an advocate to a business entity, which is also under reverse charge.
Tax = 2,50,000 x 18% = Rs 45,000, paid by the company under the reverse charge mechanism (RCM).
The company claims Rs 45,000 as input tax credit (ITC). Reference: Section 9(3) of the CGST Act and Notification 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), entries 2 and 6.
note: Entry 2 of Notification 13/2017-CT(Rate) covers legal services by advocates to a business entity and entry 6 covers director services; they are separate entries. 2,50,000 x 18% = 45,000 correct.

prompt: Turnover Rs 15 crore. A credit note dated 15 September 2026 was reported to the IRP on 20 October 2026. What happens?
completion:
The invoice registration portal (IRP) rejects it, because 35 days have passed since the credit note date. From 1 April 2025, taxpayers with turnover of Rs 10 crore or more cannot report invoices, credit notes or debit notes to the IRP after 30 days from the document date.
Days = 15 (16 to 30 September) + 20 (October) = 35 days. The last day to report was 15 October 2026.
Without an invoice reference number (IRN), the credit note is not a valid e-invoice document. Check with your tax adviser how to re-issue it with the current date, and report new documents within 30 days. Reference: GSTN advisory dated 5 November 2024 on the 30-day reporting limit.
note: 30-day IRP limit from 1 Apr 2025 for turnover of Rs 10 crore or more does cover credit notes (Taxmann quoting GSTN advisory); 35 days is correct. The completion assumed the original supply date, cited Rule 48(4) for the limit, and gave unverified re-issue advice, so these are removed.

prompt: A trading company with Rs 3.2 crore turnover last year pays a senior advocate Rs 1,25,000 for a tax appeal. Who pays GST, and how much?
completion:
The company pays GST of Rs 22,500 under reverse charge. Legal services by an advocate, including a senior advocate, to a business entity are notified for the reverse charge mechanism (RCM). Your turnover of Rs 3.2 crore is above the exemption limit, so RCM applies.
Tax = 1,25,000 x 18% = Rs 22,500.
Pay it in cash and claim it as input tax credit (ITC) if the appeal relates to your business. A business entity whose turnover in the preceding year was up to Rs 20 lakh (Rs 10 lakh in special category states) is exempt from this reverse charge. Reference: Section 9(3) of the CGST Act, Notification 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), entry 2, and Notification 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate).
note: RCM on advocate services to a business entity above the Rs 20 lakh turnover limit is correct; 1,25,000 x 18% = 22,500. The self-invoice within 30 days sentence is unverified and removed; the small-recipient exemption sits in Notification 12/2017 (entry 45), not only 13/2017.

prompt: What GST options does a goods transport agency have after 22 September 2025?
completion: A goods transport agency (GTA) has two options. Option 1 is 5% without input tax credit (ITC). The tax is paid either by a specified recipient under reverse charge or by the GTA under forward charge. Option 2 is 18% under forward charge, with full ITC. This replaced the earlier 12% option. For a freight bill of Rs 85,000: option 1 tax = 85,000 x 5% = Rs 4,250; option 2 tax = 85,000 x 18% = Rs 15,300, but the GTA then claims credit on inputs and input services used for the freight service, where eligible. The GTA must opt for forward charge by the prescribed declaration for the year. Reference: Notification 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate) and Section 9(3) of the CGST Act.
note: 5% without ITC or 18% with full ITC is as established; arithmetic 85,000 x 5% = 4,250 and x 18% = 15,300 is right. 'Credit on fuel-related services' is wrong or misleading (petrol and diesel are outside GST) so it is reworded; reference made specific.

prompt: composition dealer hu kanpur me, amazon pe saman bech sakta hu?
completion: Yes, you can sell goods through an e-commerce operator such as Amazon while staying in composition, but only within your own state. From 1 October 2023 the bar on supplying goods through an operator that collects tax at source (TCS) was removed. Outward inter-state supplies are still not allowed under composition, so a sale to another state needs regular registration. Supplying services through an operator that collects TCS remains barred. Composition dealers pay 1% on turnover in the state, file CMP-08 quarterly and GSTR-4 yearly. Reference: Section 10(2)(c) and 10(2)(d) of the CGST Act as amended by the Finance Act, 2023.
note: Finance Act 2023 removed 'goods' from the bar in Section 10(2)(d) from 1 Oct 2023, so composition dealers can supply goods intra-state through a TCS-collecting operator; services remain barred (taxclue, CA Club, EY). Notification 34/2023 could not be verified and the claim that the operator checks UP-only sales is unsupported, so both are removed.

prompt:
User: Our salon in Bandra used to charge 18%.
Assistant: After GST 2.0, beauty and physical well-being services were cut.
User: A Rs 3,800 bill: what now, and can we still claim ITC on products we buy?
completion:
Charge 5%: Rs 190 on a Rs 3,800 bill. From 22 September 2025, beauty and physical well-being services, including salons, barbers, gyms and yoga centres, are taxed at 5% without input tax credit (ITC). This rate is mandatory; you cannot choose 18% with ITC.
GST 3,800 x 5% = Rs 190. Bill total = Rs 3,990.
You can no longer claim ITC on products, rent or equipment used for these services from 22 September 2025. Retail products sold separately are taxed at their own rate. Reference: Notification 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate).
note: 5% without ITC for beauty and physical well-being services from 22 Sep 2025 is confirmed; 3,800 x 5% = 190, total 3,990. The stock-reversal sentence is unverified and removed; reference made specific.

prompt: A registered company in Thane rents a flat for its director's residence at Rs 75,000 a month from an unregistered owner. Is GST payable?
completion:
Yes. The company pays GST of Rs 13,500 a month under reverse charge. Renting of a residential dwelling to a registered person is taxable under the reverse charge mechanism (RCM), even though residential renting to an individual for personal use is exempt.
Tax = 75,000 x 18% = Rs 13,500.
Pay it in cash and report it in Table 3.1(d) of GSTR-3B. Whether input tax credit (ITC) can be claimed depends on the flat being used for the company's business under Section 16, so do not assume it is available. Reference: Notification 5/2022-Central Tax (Rate).
note: RCM at 18% on residential dwelling let to a registered person under Notification 5/2022 is correct; 75,000 x 18% = 13,500. The statement that ITC is blocked under Section 17(5)(g) for a director's residence is unsettled and unsupported, so it is replaced with a neutral line.

prompt: In last month's GSTR-3B we claimed ITC of Rs 1,12,000 but GSTR-2B supports only Rs 94,000. How do we correct it this month?
completion:
Reverse the excess of Rs 18,000 in this month's GSTR-3B, and pay interest if it was used.
Excess = 1,12,000 - 94,000 = Rs 18,000.
Show the Rs 18,000 in Table 4(B)(2) as a reversal under 'others'. If the invoices reach GSTR-2B later, re-claim them in Table 4(A)(5) and Table 4(D)(1). If the credit ledger balance fell below Rs 18,000 at any time, interest at 18% a year applies from that day to the reversal. Reference: Section 16(2)(aa) and Section 50(3) of the CGST Act, and Rule 88B.
note: Section 16(2)(aa), reversal in 4(B)(2), reclaim in 4(A)(5) with 4(D)(1), and interest under Section 50(3) at 18% via Rule 88B only if the credit was utilised are all supported; 1,12,000 - 94,000 = 18,000.

prompt: GSTR-3B for August 2023 was never filed. Can we file it now?
completion: No. From 1 October 2023, a return cannot be filed after three years from its due date. The August 2023 GSTR-3B was due on 20 September 2023, so the window closed on 20 September 2026. The GST portal blocks returns beyond the three-year limit. The tax for that month can still be assessed by the officer, with interest and penalty, so seek proper advice on settling it. Returns for later months must be filed within three years of their due dates. Reference: Section 39(11) of the CGST Act, inserted by the Finance Act, 2023, and the GSTN advisory on time-barred returns.
note: Section 39(11) from the Finance Act 2023 (in force 1 Oct 2023) bars filing after three years from the due date; GSTN enforced the block on the portal from 2025. August 2023 GSTR-3B due 20 Sep 2023, so window closed 20 Sep 2026.

prompt: GSTR-9 for 2025-26 for a company with Rs 14 crore turnover is filed 30 days late. What is the late fee?
completion:
The late fee is Rs 3,000, Rs 100 a day, as long as it stays below the turnover-linked cap. For annual returns, taxpayers with turnover above Rs 5 crore and up to Rs 20 crore pay Rs 50 a day under each act, Rs 100 in total. The cap is 0.04% of turnover in the state, 0.02% under each act.
30 days x Rs 100 = Rs 3,000.
Cap = 14,00,00,000 x 0.04% = Rs 56,000, not reached.
Pay it in cash before filing. Reference: Section 47(2) of the CGST Act and Notification 7/2023-Central Tax.
note: Notification 7/2023-CT: Rs 5 crore to Rs 20 crore pays Rs 50 per day per Act (Rs 100 total), cap 0.02% per Act (0.04% total). 30 x 100 = 3,000; cap 14 crore x 0.04% = 56,000, not reached.

prompt: Our October GSTR-1 overstated an invoice by Rs 50,000 taxable value, so we paid Rs 9,000 extra IGST in GSTR-3B. How do we get it back?
completion: Correct it through GSTR-1 in a later month, and the excess then reduces that month's liability. With the GSTR-3B hard lock, Table 3 cannot be edited downwards directly. Amend the invoice to the correct value in Table 9A of the November GSTR-1. The integrated GST (IGST) payable for November then falls by Rs 9,000, which is 50,000 x 18%. If later liability is too small to absorb it, claim a refund of excess tax paid within two years of the relevant date. Reference: Section 37(3), Section 54 of the CGST Act and Rule 89 of the CGST Rules.
note: Downward amendment through Table 9A of a later GSTR-1 with hard-locked GSTR-3B, 50,000 x 18% = 9,000, and refund under Section 54 are supported; the GSTR-1A route for an earlier period's invoice after the 3B is filed is not confirmed (a practitioner note says that route closes), so it is removed. Carry-forward of negative liability could not be confirmed (moderate confidence).

prompt: A sales manager in Thane with basic + DA of Rs 32,000 opted, jointly with the employer, to contribute on full wages from April 2026. What are the August 2026 contributions?
completion:
Both shares are Rs 3,840 on the full wage. The pension scheme (EPS) part stays capped at Rs 1,250, so the employer's provident fund (EPF) part is Rs 2,590.
Employee: 32,000 x 12% = Rs 3,840.
Employer: 32,000 x 12% = Rs 3,840.
EPS: 15,000 x 8.33% = Rs 1,249.50, rounded to Rs 1,250, because EPS stays capped at the Rs 15,000 ceiling that applied in August 2026 (before 17 September 2026).
Employer EPF: 3,840 - 1,250 = Rs 2,590.
Check: 1,250 + 2,590 = Rs 3,840. Reference: paragraph 26(6) of the EPF Scheme, 1952.
note: Contribution split arithmetic is right (EPS 15,000 x 8.33% = 1,249.50 -> 1,250; 3,840-1,250 = 2,590; Aug 2026 is before the 17 Sep ceiling change). Admin charge and EDLI lines could not be verified under the Social Security Code regime, so removed.

prompt: An employee turned 58 on 10 March 2026. His PF wage is Rs 15,000. How does the employer's share change from April?
completion:
From April, the employer's full 12% goes to the provident fund (EPF) and nothing goes to the pension scheme (EPS). EPS membership ends at 58, so no further pension contribution is made.
Employee: 15,000 x 12% = Rs 1,800.
Employer: 15,000 x 12% = Rs 1,800, all to EPF.
Before 58 the employer's split would have been EPS 15,000 x 8.33% = Rs 1,250 and EPF 1,800 - 1,250 = Rs 550.
The Rs 15,000 wage ceiling applies here, as April 2026 is before the 17 September 2026 change. Reference: Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995.
note: Rule is supported (EPS membership ends at 58; employer's full share then goes to EPF; 1,800-1,250 = 550). The month-of-birthday proration claim and the paragraph number 3 are unsupported, so removed.

prompt: An employee with a locomotor disability in Jaipur earns Rs 24,000 gross. Is she covered by ESI?
completion:
Yes. For employees with a disability, the employees' state insurance (ESI) wage limit is Rs 25,000 a month, not Rs 21,000. At Rs 24,000 she is covered.
Employee: 24,000 x 0.75% = Rs 180.
Employer: 24,000 x 3.25% = Rs 780.
Total Rs 960 a month.
A colleague without disability on the same Rs 24,000 would not be covered, because Rs 24,000 is above Rs 21,000. Reference: ESI provisions of the Code on Social Security, 2020, and the Rs 25,000 limit for persons with disability.
note: Rs 25,000 coverage limit for persons with disability is reported by Mondaq and TaxClue; arithmetic correct (180, 780, 960). ESI Act is replaced by the Code on Social Security so reference updated; due-date claim removed as unverified under the new rules.

prompt: A security guard in Surat earns Rs 4,400 a month for 25 working days (Rs 176 a day). What ESI is deducted?
completion:
No employee share is deducted, but the employer must still pay its 3.25%. Employees whose average daily wage is up to Rs 176 are exempt from paying their own employees' state insurance (ESI) contribution.
Daily wage = 4,400 / 25 = Rs 176.
Employer share = 4,400 x 3.25% = Rs 143.
Employee share = Rs 0.
If the daily wage rises to Rs 177, the employee's 0.75% starts: 4,425 x 0.75% = Rs 33.19, rounded up to Rs 34. Reference: ESIC contribution rules, daily wage limit of Rs 176 for the employee's share.
note: Rs 176 average daily wage exemption confirmed on ESIC site (employer share still payable). 4,400/25 = 176; 4,400 x 3.25% = 143; 4,425 x 0.75% = 33.19 -> 34 with round-up. Section 42 citation replaced by a generic reference because the Act has been replaced.

prompt: esi rounding off rule? 0.75% of 19,830 comes 148.725
completion:
Round up to the next whole rupee. The employee's employees' state insurance (ESI) share becomes Rs 149, not Rs 148.73.
Employee: 19,830 x 0.75% = Rs 148.725, rounded up to Rs 149.
Employer: 19,830 x 3.25% = Rs 644.475, rounded up to Rs 645.
Total deposited = 149 + 645 = Rs 794.
Each share is rounded up to the next higher rupee, never down. Reference: Rule 19 of the Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026.
note: Each share is rounded up to the next higher rupee (Rule 19, Social Security (Central) Rules 2026, per TaxClue; consistent with long-standing ESIC practice). Arithmetic: 148.725 -> 149; 644.475 -> 645; total 794. Regulation 31 of the 1950 Regulations is replaced, so reference updated.

prompt:
User: Our FnF for an exiting employee shows notice recovery of Rs 40,000.
Assistant: Notice pay is recovered under the contract.
User: Do we have to charge GST on that Rs 40,000?
completion: No. CBIC has clarified that notice pay recovered from a departing employee is not consideration for any supply, so GST is not charged. It is an adjustment under the employment contract, and services by an employee to an employer are outside GST. Show the Rs 40,000 as a deduction in the full and final settlement, and do not raise a tax invoice or add GST on top. Reference: CBIC Circular 178/10/2022-GST dated 3 August 2022 and Schedule III para 1 of the CGST Act.
note: CBIC Circular 178/10/2022-GST (3 Aug 2022) confirms notice pay recovery from employees is not consideration for a supply. The sentence about older advance rulings was unverified, so removed.

prompt:
User: Our employee works in Maharashtra.
Assistant: Professional tax applies under the Maharashtra law.
User: What is the monthly slab for a man earning Rs 42,000?
completion:
For a man earning Rs 42,000 a month in Maharashtra, professional tax is Rs 200 a month, with Rs 300 in February, totalling Rs 2,500 a year.
Months: 11 x 200 = Rs 2,200; February = Rs 300; total = Rs 2,500.
Salaries up to Rs 7,500 are nil and Rs 7,501 to Rs 10,000 attract Rs 175, so Rs 42,000 falls in the top slab. Deduct it monthly from salary and deposit it under the employer's professional tax registration (PTRC) by the state due date. Reference: Maharashtra State Tax on Professions, Trades, Callings and Employments Act, 1975, Schedule I.
note: Men's slab (Rs 200, Rs 300 in Feb, 11 x 200 + 300 = 2,500) is established. Women's Rs 25,000 exemption is unconfirmed, so that sentence and the hedge were removed.

prompt:
User: I pay my mother Rs 30,000 a month rent for the flat I live in.
Assistant: Rent paid to a parent can qualify for HRA if it is genuine.
User: Does my employer need anything special from me?
completion: Yes. Give your employer rent receipts and your mother's PAN, and declare the landlord details and your relationship to her in the HRA declaration (Form 124 from 1 April 2026). Your rent is 30,000 x 12 = Rs 3,60,000 a year, above Rs 1,00,000, so the landlord's PAN is required to claim house rent allowance (HRA) exemption in payroll. Your mother must show the Rs 3,60,000 as rental income in her own return. The flat should be owned by her, not you, and you must actually pay her, preferably by bank transfer, with a rent agreement as support. HRA exemption is available only under the old regime; in the new regime HRA is fully taxable. Reference: Income-tax Act, 2025 and Income-tax Rules, 2026.
note: Landlord PAN above Rs 1 lakh annual rent and relationship disclosure continue under Income-tax Rules 2026 (Form 124); HRA only in old regime. As of Nov 2026 the reference to the 1961 Act and the unverified circular should go. 30,000 x 12 = 3,60,000.

prompt: company car above 1.6 litre with driver, used for office and personal both. perquisite per month fy 25-26?
completion:
The perquisite is Rs 3,300 a month, Rs 39,600 a year. For a car with engine above 1.6 litres used for both official and personal purposes, with the employer bearing running costs, the value is Rs 2,400 a month. A chauffeur adds Rs 900 a month.
Monthly = 2,400 + 900 = Rs 3,300.
Annual = 3,300 x 12 = Rs 39,600, taxable in both regimes.
For a car up to 1.6 litres the base is Rs 1,800. If the car is used only for official duty, with records kept, there is no perquisite. Reference: Rule 3(2) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, for financial year 2025-26.
note: Old Rule 3(2) values for FY 2025-26: Rs 2,400 (above 1.6 L, employer bears costs, mixed use) + Rs 900 chauffeur = 3,300; x 12 = 39,600; up to 1.6 L is Rs 1,800. The draft increases apply from FY 2026-27 only.

prompt: An employer gave a Diwali gift voucher of Rs 5,000 in FY 2025-26. Is it taxable? What about Rs 4,999?
completion: The Rs 5,000 voucher is taxable in full, while Rs 4,999 is tax-free. Gifts and vouchers from the employer are valued at nil only if their aggregate value in the year is below Rs 5,000. At Rs 5,000 the aggregate is not below the limit, so the whole Rs 5,000 is a perquisite, not just the excess. At Rs 4,999 the perquisite is nil. Add any other gifts in the year to the aggregate before applying the test. Reference: Rule 3(7)(iv) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, for financial year 2025-26.
note: Rule 3(7)(iv) proviso: nil only where value is below Rs 5,000 in aggregate in the year; otherwise the perquisite is the cost to employer, i.e. the whole amount. Rs 5,000 is not below Rs 5,000. The Rs 15,000 draft threshold applies from FY 2026-27.

prompt: A sugar mill in Kolhapur runs seasonally. A worker on Rs 900 a day worked 6 seasons. What gratuity is due?
completion:
Gratuity is Rs 37,800, at seven days' wages for each season. Workers in a seasonal establishment, one that does not work all year, get gratuity at seven days' wages for each season, not 15 days for each year.
Gratuity = 7 x 900 x 6 = Rs 37,800.
The worker must have worked in each counted season under the rules for seasonal service. If the mill were not seasonal, the 15/26 formula would apply. Reference: Section 53 of the Code on Social Security, 2020 (formerly the proviso to Section 4(2) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972).
note: Seven days' wages per season for seasonal establishments is carried into Section 53 of the Code on Social Security (same as proviso to old Section 4(2)); 7 x 900 x 6 = 37,800 is correct.

prompt: An employee was dismissed for misconduct on Monday 9 November 2026. Does the two-day FnF rule still apply?
completion: Yes. The two-working-day rule covers dismissal, removal and retrenchment as well as resignation. Pay his earned wages and other wage dues by Wednesday 11 November 2026. Dismissal does not let the employer hold back earned wages. Gratuity may be forfeited only in specific cases, such as damage to property, riotous conduct or an offence involving moral turpitude, and only to the extent allowed. Ordinary misconduct does not forfeit it. Reference: Section 17(2) of the Code on Wages, 2019 and Section 53 of the Code on Social Security, 2020.
note: Monday 9 Nov 2026 is correct; two working days gives Wednesday 11 Nov. Section 17(2) covers dismissal/removal; gratuity forfeiture limited to damage, riotous conduct/violence, moral-turpitude offence is consistent with the Code's Section 53 (carried over from 4(6)). Moderate confidence on forfeiture wording, which is hedged in the row.

prompt: fnf still pending after 3 weeks, hr says accounts busy. what can the ex employee do
completion: The employer is already in breach, because wages are due within two working days of exit. The former employee can first send a written demand to HR and the company's registered office, listing the dues. If it stays unpaid, he can file a claim before the claims authority under the Code on Wages, which can order payment and add compensation of up to ten times the amount claimed. Delayed gratuity carries simple interest from the date it became payable until it is paid. Keep the resignation acceptance, relieving letter and salary slips as evidence. Reference: Sections 17(2) and 45 of the Code on Wages, 2019 and Section 56(4) of the Code on Social Security, 2020.
note: Section 45 (claims before authority, compensation up to ten times the claim) is confirmed. But the gratuity interest provision is Section 56(4) of the Code on Social Security, and 'controlling authority' naming is unverified, so it is reworded.

prompt: What is the most bonus an employer must pay, and the least?
completion:
The minimum bonus is 8.33% of wages earned (or Rs 100 if higher), and the maximum is 20%, depending on the allocable surplus of the establishment. Wages for bonus are capped at Rs 7,000 a month or the minimum wage, whichever is higher, for employees earning up to Rs 21,000. For example, on a calculation wage of Rs 11,000 a month:
Minimum = 11,000 x 12 x 8.33% = Rs 10,995.60, rounded to Rs 10,996.
Maximum = 11,000 x 12 x 20% = Rs 26,400.
Anything paid above 20% is not statutory bonus. Reference: Section 26 of the Code on Wages, 2019.
note: Figures and arithmetic correct (11,000 x 12 x 8.33% = 10,995.60; x 20% = 26,400). Section 26 holds minimum, 20% maximum and ceiling; Section 27 is proportionate reduction, so it is removed.

prompt: A factory retrenches a worker with 7 years 8 months' service and last wages Rs 26,000. What retrenchment compensation is due?
completion:
Retrenchment compensation is Rs 1,20,000, at 15 days' average pay for each completed year of service or part over six months.
Service = 7 years 8 months = 8 years.
Compensation = 26,000 x 15 / 26 x 8 = 15,000 x 8 = Rs 1,20,000.
Gratuity is payable separately. The employer also has to contribute to the worker re-skilling fund for him, at the rate notified (15 days' last drawn wages). Reference: Sections 70 and 83 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.
note: Section 70 (15 days' average pay per completed year or part over six months) and Section 83 (re-skilling fund) are supported; arithmetic 26,000 x 15/26 x 8 = 1,20,000 is correct. The Section 10(10B) Income-tax Act 1961 reference and Rs 5 lakh exemption is outdated after 1 Apr 2026 and unverified under the 2025 Act, so the tax sentence is removed; reskilling rate hedged as notified.

prompt: By when must statutory bonus for the accounting year ending 31 March 2026 be paid?
completion: Pay it by 30 November 2026, within eight months of the close of the accounting year. The time can be extended only by the appropriate government on an application, for up to two years. An employee who left during the year is still owed bonus for the months worked, if he worked at least 30 days. For example, a leaver with bonus wages of Rs 7,000 a month for 9 months is owed 7,000 x 9 x 8.33% = Rs 5,247.90, rounded to Rs 5,248, by the same date. Reference: the payment-time provision for bonus in the Code on Wages, 2019 (formerly Section 19 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965).
note: Section 39 of the Code on Wages: eight months from close of accounting year (31 Mar 2026 -> 30 Nov 2026), extension up to two years in total by the appropriate government; 30-day minimum eligibility; 7,000 x 9 x 8.33% = 5,247.90 correct.

prompt: Can a state fix a minimum wage below the national floor wage?
completion: No. The central government fixes a floor wage, and state governments cannot fix minimum wages below it. A state with a current minimum above the floor cannot reduce it. Employers must pay the higher of the notified state minimum for the category and area, or any wage set by agreement. For example, if a state's unskilled rate is Rs 14,800, any notified floor below that does not lower what the employer pays. Check both the state notification and the floor-wage notification for your sector. Reference: Section 9 of the Code on Wages, 2019.
note: Floor wage is in Section 9 of the Code on Wages; minimum rates fixed by the appropriate Government cannot be below the floor wage and an existing higher state rate cannot be reduced.

prompt: Our state revises the variable DA in minimum wages every April and October. A worker's minimum rose from Rs 14,600 to Rs 15,050 from 1 October 2026, but payroll still pays Rs 14,600. What now?
completion:
Pay the revised minimum from 1 October 2026 and clear the arrears.
Arrears for October = 15,050 - 14,600 = Rs 450.
If the correction is made only in December payroll, arrears = 450 x 3 = Rs 1,350 (October, November, December).
Also recompute provident fund (PF) and employees' state insurance (ESI) on the higher wage for those months and pay the difference.
Paying below the notified minimum wage is a breach of the Code on Wages, and the worker can claim the shortfall. Set a payroll alert for each revision date in every state you operate in.
Reference: Section 6 of the Code on Wages, 2019 (fixation of minimum wages).
note: Arithmetic is right (450 a month, 3 x 450 = 1,350 if fixed in December payroll). Section 45 reference is unverified; Section 6 is fixation of minimum wages. Removed the unsupported compensation claim and Section 45.

prompt: ESI contribution of Rs 48,000 for August 2026 was paid 45 days late. What is the interest?
completion:
Interest is Rs 710, at 12% a year simple interest for each day of delay.
Interest = 48,000 x 12% x 45 / 365 = Rs 710.14, rounded to Rs 710.
Damages may also be levied by order of the ESI Corporation, on a graded scale by length of delay, and cannot exceed the arrears of contribution. Pay the contribution and interest together through the employees' state insurance (ESI) portal. Repeated delays can lead to prosecution.
Reference: Regulations 31A and 31C of the ESI (General) Regulations, 1950.
note: Interest at 12% a year for each day (Regulation 31A) confirmed; 48,000 x 12% x 45/365 = 710.14. The 'up to 25% a year' damages figure and its table were not verified (damages are capped by the arrears under Section 85B), so the damages sentence is made generic.

prompt: An engineering firm in Gurugram takes 12 trainees under the Apprentices Act, 1961, on a stipend of Rs 18,000 each. Are PF and ESI deductible?
completion:
No. Apprentices engaged under the Apprentices Act, 1961, are excluded from the definition of employee in the Code on Social Security, 2020, so no provident fund (PF) or employees' state insurance (ESI) contributions are deducted from their stipend of Rs 18,000.
Keep the apprenticeship contracts registered on the apprenticeship portal and follow the stipend and other duties under the Apprentices Act.
If a trainee is not engaged under that Act, he is an ordinary employee and PF and ESI apply, subject to the wage ceilings. An apprentice later hired on regular rolls is covered from the date of employment.
Reference: Code on Social Security, 2020 (definition of employee) and the Apprentices Act, 1961.
note: Code on Social Security 'employee' definition excludes apprentices under the Apprentices Act 1961 (secondary source: no PF/ESI on stipend). The 'insurance under that scheme' claim is unsupported and is removed; the section number is not cited.

prompt: Is statutory bonus mandatory for a firm with 16 employees?
completion:
No. The statutory bonus provisions of the Code on Wages, 2019 apply only to establishments employing 20 or more employees. A firm with 16 employees is outside the mandatory bonus scheme.
The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 was repealed and replaced by the Code from 21 November 2025, and the 20-employee threshold continues.
If the firm pays a bonus anyway, it is a voluntary payment on the terms of the employment contract or company policy, and it should be written down so that the amount and the conditions are clear. If headcount reaches 20 at any point, review the position again.
Reference: Code on Wages, 2019, Chapter IV (bonus).
note: Code on Wages bonus chapter (Chapter IV, replaced the Payment of Bonus Act from 21 Nov 2025) applies to establishments with 20 or more employees; sources place the threshold in Section 26 or 41, so no section cited. The claims about notification extension and states applying it to 10+ employees are unsupported and removed.

prompt: Can we deduct the cost of a broken laptop worth Rs 45,000 from an employee's salary of Rs 30,000 in one month?
completion: No, not in one month. Deductions from wages are allowed only for listed reasons, such as damage or loss caused by the employee's default, after giving him a chance to explain. Total deductions in a wage period cannot exceed 50% of wages, so no more than Rs 15,000 a month here. Recover the Rs 45,000 over at least three months, Rs 15,000 a month, and keep a record of the inquiry. Deducting the whole amount at once would breach the Code. Reference: Section 18 of the Code on Wages, 2019.
note: Section 18 allows deductions only as authorised, total deductions in a wage period capped at 50% of wages (Section 18(3)); 50% of 30,000 = 15,000 and 45,000 / 15,000 = 3 months.

prompt: Can a factory engage contract workers for its core production activity?
completion: Generally no. The labour codes restrict engaging contract labour in core activities, with exceptions: where the normal functioning is such that the work is done through contractors, where the work is not full-time, or where there is a sudden increase in work that must be finished in a set time. Non-core activities, such as sanitation, security, canteen and loading, may use contractors. A factory using contract workers for core production should either bring them on rolls or justify the exception in writing. Reference: Section 57 of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.
note: OSH Code Section 57 restricts contract labour in core activities with the three standard exceptions; non-core activities such as canteen, security and sanitation are carved out.

prompt: A food-delivery aggregator wants to know its social security contribution for gig workers.
completion: Aggregators contribute 1% to 2% of their annual turnover to the gig and platform workers' social security fund, capped at 5% of the amount paid to gig and platform workers. The exact rate is set by notification. For example, an aggregator with turnover of Rs 400 crore and gig payouts of Rs 120 crore, at a 1% rate, contributes Rs 4 crore. That is below the cap of 5% of Rs 120 crore, Rs 6 crore. Gig workers must be registered on the national portal to receive benefits. Reference: Section 114 of the Code on Social Security, 2020.
note: Section 114 of the Code on Social Security: aggregator contribution of 1-2% of annual turnover, capped at 5% of amount paid or payable to gig and platform workers. Example: 1% x 400 crore = 4 crore; cap 5% x 120 crore = 6 crore, correct.

prompt: An employee's PF was not deducted for 5 months by mistake. Can we recover the employee's share from him now?
completion:
Generally no. The employer must first pay both shares to the provident fund (PF), and the employee's share can be recovered only by deduction from wages for the period it relates to. A share missed through a mistake in earlier months cannot normally be deducted later from future wages.
For example, if each share was Rs 1,800 a month, the employee share for 5 months = 1,800 x 5 = Rs 9,000, and the employer's own share is another Rs 9,000, so the employer deposits Rs 18,000 in all.
The delayed deposit also attracts interest and damages. Fix the payroll master now so deductions run correctly from this month.
Reference: paragraphs 30 and 32 of the EPF Scheme, 1952.
note: Completion contradicts itself ('Only from the next wage payments' then 'cannot'). Para 30(1) requires employer to pay both shares first; para 32 allows recovery only by deduction from wages, and a narrow proviso for clerical error has been read not to allow recovery from future wages. Arithmetic 1,800 x 5 = 9,000 is correct.

prompt: A firm's Q2 Form 138 for tax year 2026-27 shows a PAN mismatch for 3 employees. What should we do?
completion:
File a correction statement for Q2 with the correct PANs, after verifying them on the PAN verification utility. A wrong PAN means the tax deducted at source (TDS) is not credited to the employee, and the deductor may receive a default notice. Collect PAN cards or verified copies from the three employees, correct the deductee details, and resubmit. Then reconcile the statement with the challans before the next quarter's filing.
For the three employees, the credit will appear in their Form 130 and tax credit statement only after the correction is processed.
Reference: the TDS statement provisions of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (salary TDS, Form 138).
note: Practice is right (file correction statement with verified PANs). The specific citation of Section 392 as the basis for correction statements could not be verified, so the reference line is replaced with a general one; 'short-deduction demand' wording softened.

prompt:
User: Our plant in Vapi employs 300 workers, all through two contractors.
Assistant: As principal employer you carry statutory liabilities.
User: Do we need a licence or registration for using contractors?
completion:
Yes, the contractors need a licence; you as principal employer must make sure they hold one.
With 300 workers engaged through contractors, Part I of Chapter XI of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 applies (50 or more contract workers), and each contractor must hold a licence from the designated authority. Your establishment should also be registered under the Code.
Using an unlicensed contractor is a contravention, and an indemnity clause does not cure it. You are directly responsible for the welfare facilities for contract workers and must pay wages if a contractor fails to pay or pays short, recovering it from the contractor.
Reference: Sections 45, 47, 53, 54 and 55 of the OSH Code, 2020.
note: OSH Code Chapter XI Part I applies at 50 or more contract labour (Section 45); contractor licence Section 47; principal employer is directly responsible for welfare facilities (Section 53) and liable for unpaid wages on contractor default (Section 55). The PF/ESI default claim and the canteen threshold ('with 300 workers') were not verified and are removed.

prompt:
User: We export software services from Bengaluru under LUT and our turnover is Rs 14 crore.
Assistant: Export invoices are e-invoices for you.
User: Even for services with zero tax? And what supply type?
completion: Yes. Export of services under a letter of undertaking (LUT), with zero integrated GST (IGST), still needs an invoice reference number (IRN). E-invoicing covers all business-to-business supplies, including exports of goods and services, for taxpayers over the Rs 5 crore turnover limit. Use supply type 'export without payment' (EXPWOP). Show the foreign recipient's details with pseudo GSTIN 'URP' and place of supply '96' for other countries. Your turnover is above Rs 10 crore, so report within 30 days of the invoice date. Reference: Rule 48(4) of the CGST Rules.
note: E-invoicing covers B2B exports above Rs 5 crore; EXPWOP, buyer GSTIN URP and place of supply 96 are the standard export fields; GSTN advisory extends the 30-day IRP reporting limit to AATO of Rs 10 crore and above from 1 April 2025, so Rs 14 crore is covered.
